articles.title: Khor Mor drone attack raises fears over Iraq’s energy security
articles.summary: Drone strike disrupts electricity supply in Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region, renewing concerns about armed groups.
articles.body:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has drawn attention to the security challenges facing the country’s energy sector, amid escalating regional tensions and domestic political disagreements over restricting weapons to state control.

The attack in Sulaimaniyah governorate late on Sunday sparked a fire and forced the suspension of gas supplies to several power stations, initially reducing electricity generation in areas administered by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) by between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts, according to regional officials.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the formation of a joint investigative committee with KRG authorities to determine who was behind the attack.

No group has claimed responsibility, but the attack comes as regional tensions are heightened due to the US-Israel war on Iran, with Baghdad facing pressure to bring weapons held by predominantly pro-Iranian Shia armed factions under state control . KRG authorities have blamed Iran-backed groups in Iraq for previous attacks on the field in recent years.

The attack also comes days after the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) announced its withdrawal from the KRG , deepening a political crisis with its rival, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).

Mohammed Amer, a political science academic and a member of the KDP, said the Khor Mor attack represents a genuine test of the Iraqi state’s sovereignty and its ability to rein in armed groups operating outside its control, and protect its territory and vital facilities.

“The [federal Iraqi] government bears responsibility for protecting Iraqi territory and airspace,” Amer told Al Jazeera. “The repeated targeting of energy sources in the Kurdistan Region also requires it to hold accountable the parties and factions behind these attacks, and to question the authorities responsible for the areas from which they are launched.”

Amer urged the Iraqi government to accelerate efforts to bring weapons under state control, warning that repeated attacks coud deter foreign investment in Iraq’s energy industry.

“These strikes target foreign investment in Iraq’s energy sector, particularly as the Khor Mor field has been targeted many times using drones and missiles,” he said. “There are factions that declare their loyalty to Iran and not to the Iraqi state, and this raises questions about the government’s ability to impose its authority and sovereignty over all Iraqi territory.”

Strategic affairs researcher Kadhim Yawer also linked the attack to regional tensions, with fears continuing that the war between the United States and Iran may escalate once again in the coming days and weeks.

“The strategic purpose of targeting the Khor Mor field at this time is primarily due to external factors linked to the escalation of the conflict between Iran and the US, as well as the desire to inflict economic damage on the Kurdistan Region and Iraq in general,” Yawer said.

He said that the dispute over disarming militias, combined with worsening divisions between the KDP and the PUK, could add to the economic pressure on the region. That comes at a time when, according to Yawer, the field’s importance could grow as the KRG seeks to expand gas production and potentially reach new markets.

Yawer argued that the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces from Iraq had created additional security challenges, particularly as some political forces – including parliamentarians – continue to not support the full disarmament of militias, allowing them more freedom to operate.

Internal disputes raise fears of wider conflict

Political researcher Ghanem al-Abed pointed to the timing of the attack, which came as the political dispute between the KDP and the PUK intensified and Baghdad faced resistance from armed groups over its disarmament plans.

“The notable point about the timing of the targeting of the Khor Mor field is that it coincides with political disagreements between the KDP and the PUK, as well as the escalating disagreements between the Iraqi prime minister and some armed factions over handing their weapons to the state,” he said.

The Reuters news agency has reported that the attack originated from the Tuz Khurmatu area of Salah al-Din governorate, outside of northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region – although neither the launch location nor the perpetrators have been officially established so far. Al-Abed called on the Iraqi central government to identify those responsible and hold them accountable.

Al-Abed said the economic consequences of further attacks could extend beyond areas administered by the KRG, given the field’s role in electricity generation in the neighbouring governorates of Kirkuk and Nineveh.

“The Iraqi government must announce the identity of the parties seeking to destroy the country’s economy and hold them accountable,” he said. “The situation in Iraq could explode at any moment because some armed factions are not complying with the demand to hand over their weapons to the state. If war breaks out again between Iran and the US, these factions may intervene in the confrontation, and Iraq could then turn into a battlefield.”

articles.title: Traffic disruption warning as Dublin prepares to host EU meetings
articles.summary: Irish police say it is going to be the largest security operation in the history of the state.
articles.body:
The public is being warned to expect traffic disruption in Dublin this week, as the Irish capital hosts two major European Union presidency events on Thursday and Friday.

The Republic of Ireland has been chairing the EU presidency since 1 July and will continue to do so until 31 December.

This has led to Ireland being the meeting place for many political leaders from across the EU in recent months.

The two main showpieces of the EU presidency will be a meeting of the European Political Community (EPC) on Thursday 12 November and an informal meeting of the European Council the following day.

Some 50 international leaders will attend a meeting of the EPC, while leaders from the 27 EU member states, as well as some other international leaders, will remain in Dublin for Friday's meeting.

The EPC will take place in the Convention Centre Dublin, with a formal dinner in the National Gallery of Ireland on Thursday evening.

The informal European Council meeting will take place in the convention centre on Friday.

Arrivals and departures for these events will take place at Dublin Airport and Casement Aerodrome.

The security operation for the two meetings will be the largest in the state's history, according to An Garda Síochána (Irish police).

Supt Liam Geraghty said there had been "intense and extensive planning" between the force and local authorities, transport companies as well as businesses and residents in key locations.

"Our appeal is to advise the public of the significant traffic disruptions that will take place in order to put that policing and security operation in place," he said.

He described the policing and security operation as being bigger than those put on for any US presidential visit.

The policing operation will begin and increase incrementally from Tuesday 10 November and Wednesday.

Gardaí expect to put in place temporary traffic restrictions across the wider Dublin region to facilitate security motorcycle escorts from Dublin Airport and Casement Aerodrome to Dublin city centre.

The highest impact of these restrictions will be:

• 13:00 (local time, 13:00 GMT) -23:00 Wednesday 11 November, airports to city centre

• 07:00-11:00 Thursday 12 November, airports to city centre/in city centre

• 15:00-23:00 Thursday 12 November, city centre

• 07:00-11:00 Friday 13 November, city centre

• 13:00-20:00 Friday 13 November, city centre to airports

The M50 motorway and Dublin Port Tunnel are not expected to be directly affected.

Political leaders will arrive and depart from Dublin Airport during 11, 12 and 13 November.

The highest impact of these arrivals/departures will be:

Gardaí said normal operations would continue at Dublin Airport, with departures and arrival roads for terminals one and two being unaffected.

But members of the public who are travelling have been warned to allow extra time to arrive at the airport during the peak times.

Traffic restrictions will be in place at Dunbro between R108 and R122.

Additional police patrols will be in place along perimeter roads of Dublin Airport including the Naul Road, R108, R132 and Old Airport Road.

Access to the aircraft viewing stands on the R108 and Naul Road adjacent to Dublin Airport will be restricted.

Casement Aerodrome at Baldonnel, the Irish military airbase, will see heads of state or government arrive and depart.

The highest level of disruption will be during:

Perimeter roads will be subject to additional patrols and traffic restrictions. Parking and stopping on perimeter roads will be restricted.

Former One Direction singer Niall Horan is performing at the 3Arena for four nights, 9, 10, 12 and 13 November.

The 3Arena will be outside of the security cordon for this operation, but there will be no east/west traffic on North Wall Quay from 10-13 November.

Cars will be able to access the 3Arena along Seville Place/Sherriff Street Upper, East Wall Road and across Tom Clarke Toll Bridge at all times.

Luas operations will continue as normal on 10 November 2026, but there will be no Luas services to the 3Arena on the 12 and 13 November.

A restricted number of special Luas services will be facilitated after the event on the 12 and 13 November.

There will be no pedestrian access along North Wall Quay on 12 and 13 November 2026.

The policing operation will begin on Tuesday and a security cordon will be established around the Convention Centre Dublin from 07:00, including barriers and no-parking restrictions.

On Wednesday, a security cordon will be established around the National Gallery of Ireland from 07:00, including barriers and no-parking restrictions.

Traffic and parking restrictions may be implemented in the vicinity of hotels associated with these meetings from 07:00 until late Friday morning across Dublin south and north city centre.

A wider security cordon and extended traffic management cordon will be established around the Convention Centre Dublin from 20:00 on Wednesday until Friday evening.

Samuel Beckett Bridge will be closed to traffic from 20:00, with north/south traffic across Samuel Beckett Bridge being diverted from approach roads.

Access to residents and businesses will remain open, with security checks

Gardaí said it could be expected that there will be significant road closures in this area, at times between 15:00-1900 on Thursday.

articles.title: After thieves took about 30 of his village’s 18th-century wall stones in Rufford, Lancashire, councillor Matt Smith hid an Apple AirTag inside a loose one; when it moved overnight, police tracked down the thief
articles.summary: An English mayor was fed up with watching 300-year-old coping stones vanish from an 18th-century ancient wall one by one.
articles.body: An English mayor was fed up with watching 300-year-old coping stones vanish from an 18th-century ancient wall one by one. With no cameras around, pointing fingers or catching the thief seemed like an impossible task. Matt Smith said people living near Rufford Old Hall in Lancashire "were getting a bit miffed" with stones being taken from the historic boundary wall, spread along a half-mile stretch of road which connects Holmeswood and Rufford in October 2025.Locals noticed the wall was first attacked and stones were taken in May, with two further raids taking place in June and October. "We looked at installing some CCTV, but it costs and with the wall being attacked at random places at random times, in a half-mile stretch of wall, it was going to be hard to cover that area," the parish councillor said. He said the parish council "put some lovely 'smile, you're on camera' signs up and unfortunately that didn't deter them".Thus, to investigate and possibly find a conclusion, he put an Apple AirTag, a coin-sized tracking device, inside one of the stones. "I devised a plan and spoke with the owners," he said. He said he and the owners "noticed it was the smaller of the stones that were being taken," so they decided to put a tracking device in what they believed would be the next stone to go.He said he drilled into one of the smaller coping stones and placed an Apple AirTag inside before he "patched up the core, ground it up, put a bit of resin in" and placed it back on the wall.About four weeks later, his phone began to ping with the tracking device on the move to an address in Winstanley in Wigan. He contacted the police, who went to the address and made an arrest. The coping stones were later returned and the "extremely grateful" residents rebuilt the wall.According to a BBC report, the tracker led police to an address in Wigan and eventually saw a man plead guilty to two counts of theft and one count of handling stolen goods at Wigan Magistrates' Court in October. Craig Barker, 41, from Wigan, pleaded guilty to theft and handling stolen goods and was given a 12-month sentence, suspended for 22 months in October. On the scene, police found a substantial number of coping stones from the vandalised wall, reportedly worth around £7,000 / $9,300—but Smith claimed dozens of others were also found from across the country, making the estimated total value up to £40,000.Speaking after the case, PC Sean Dalby said it highlighted "the strong relationships we have developed with our communities and demonstrates the effectiveness of working together to tackle rural and heritage crime". "I would like to thank the local residents for their support throughout the investigation, as well as those who gave their time to rebuild the wall free of charge," he added.The wall is thought to have been built around 1730 for the historic Grade II-listed Rufford New Hall, which was later converted into a hospital in the 1900s, and later into apartments. “It was a great feeling to know we had found the man responsible. I’m glad we stood up and didn’t just tolerate it,” said Smith.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: House martin nests scheme expanded in Hampshire to combat decline
articles.summary: The artificial nests are more robust than the endangered migratory birds' own mud creations.
articles.body:
Up to 900 artificial nest "cups" for threatened house martins are set to be installed in Hampshire as part of a conservation project.

The birds migrate from Africa each spring and are on the UK's Red List of endangered bird species. They are thought to have suffered from a lack of wet mud to build nests during the extreme heat in the summer.

Following a pilot project, The Hampshire House Martins Project is offering free cups which save the birds time and energy compared to building their own mud nests.

Project co-ordinator Nigel Matthews encouraged residents, schools and businesses to apply for the free artificial nests "to give these remarkable birds a safe place to raise their young".

Between 1995 and 2024, the UK House Martin population fell by 40%, partly due to poor breeding success.

The birds build distinctive cup-shaped nests beneath the roofs of houses and other buildings, carrying around 1,000 pellets of soft mud to complete each one.

Each April and May, house martins return from Africa to spend the summer in the UK.

The birds often form colonies with several nests in close proximity.

The decline in numbers has been blamed on a fall in quantities of insects, as well as hotter, drier weather - as seen during the summer of 2026 - resulting in less wet mud available for nest building.

Modern homes tending to have uPVC soffits also makes it difficult for mud nests to adhere.

Last year the Hampshire Ornithological Society initiative launched a survey, allowing members of the public to record house martin nest locations .

The group is now looking for additional properties where artificial nests will be provided and fitted free of charge - thought to be the biggest such project in the country.

During the project's pilot, 249 artificial nest cups were installed on buildings close to known nesting sites across northern and eastern Hampshire.

Twenty seven were used by house martins this summer, more than the project team had expected.

Keith Betton, chair of Hampshire Ornithological Society, said: "The response to the first pilot stage of this project showed how strongly people across Hampshire want to help house martins.

"This next phase turns what we have learnt into action by offering hundreds more safe, ready-made nests.

"It gives homeowners, schools and businesses a simple, practical way to support the recovery of this threatened bird."

To quality for a cup, which are provided and installed for free, properties must be within 1km (0.6 miles) of a previously recorded house martin nest.

Host buildings must have suitable overhanging eaves at second story level, between four and seven metres from the ground.

Applications for the nest cups can be made on the Hampshire House Martins Project website.

articles.title: A historic election for Jain Americans: From a small community to a national voice
articles.summary: Tuesday, November 3, was a remarkable day for Indian Americans.
articles.body: Tuesday, November 3, was a remarkable day for Indian Americans. The community gained two new members of Congress, celebrated victories in state and local elections, and witnessed a historic breakthrough in Los Angeles, the city I have called home for the past four decades.Indian American Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass to become mayor of America's second-largest city. Together with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, she represents the growing presence of Indian Americans in the leadership of major American cities.These victories came amid increasingly hostile rhetoric from elements of the far right, including attacks on Indian immigrants, professionals and religious traditions. Against that backdrop, the results offered a powerful reminder of America's democratic promise.For me, as a Jain American, the congressional victories of Pia Dandiya in Florida and Dr. Amish Shah in Arizona carry particular significance.Dandiya, a former educator and technology executive, won Florida's 22nd Congressional District. Shah, a physician and former Arizona state legislator who has spoken proudly of his Jain heritage, won Arizona's 1st Congressional District.Both are Democrats who entered politics after establishing successful professional careers, reflecting a growing commitment to public service among Indian Americans.It is difficult to overstate what meaningful political representation means to a community as small as ours.Estimates place the Jain American population at approximately 160,000, a tiny fraction of the American population. To put that in perspective, Los Angeles County alone has approximately 9.7 million residents. Our entire community amounts to roughly 1.6 percent of that county's population.Jainism is among the world's oldest living religious traditions, with roots extending back thousands of years in India. Yet its followers remain relatively few, with the overwhelming majority living in India.For generations, Jain Americans have been better known for their achievements in business, medicine, education and philanthropy than for their participation in electoral politics.We have built temples, community centers and educational institutions across the United States. We have supported universities, hospitals and charitable causes. But political representation in this country has remained largely beyond our reach.For a community as small as ours, seeing a Jain American elected to Congress is the political equivalent of landing a person on the moon. It represents a breakthrough that expands our understanding of what is possible.Consider the journeys of Dandiya and Shah.Born and raised in Palm Beach County, Florida, to immigrant parents from India, Dandiya began her career as a teacher before becoming a high school principal. She subsequently served as a White House Fellow at the Department of Education and worked at Apple on public-sector initiatives.Her campaign emphasized education, affordability, healthcare and expanding opportunities for working families.Shah, meanwhile, is a Chicago-born physician whose parents immigrated from India in the 1960s. His father is Jain and his mother Hindu. Shah has spoken about the influence of Jain teachings, including nonviolence, non-materialism and respect for different perspectives, on his personal and political outlook.Before winning election to Congress, he served in the Arizona House of Representatives, focusing on healthcare and other public policy issues.Their victories demonstrate that candidates from relatively small communities can build broad electoral coalitions.Neither Dandiya nor Shah could have won by relying exclusively on Indian American voters, much less Jain American voters. They had to appeal to Americans of different races, religions, backgrounds and political traditions. That is an essential lesson about democratic representation.Jainism teaches principles that have profound relevance to contemporary society.Ahimsa, or nonviolence, encourages respect for all living beings.Anekantavada recognizes that truth is multifaceted and that no individual possesses a monopoly on wisdom.Aparigraha, or non-possessiveness, encourages restraint and reminds us that material accumulation should not become the sole purpose of life.These principles do not belong to any political party, nor do they dictate positions on every public policy question. But they offer a moral framework that can enrich American public life.At a time of increasing political polarization, the Jain emphasis on understanding multiple perspectives is particularly relevant.Nonviolence challenges us to reject hatred and intimidation, while our tradition of service reminds us that personal success carries responsibilities toward the wider community.Jain Americans should not expect elected officials who share their heritage to represent only Jain interests. Their responsibility is to serve everyone in their districts. That, too, is consistent with our values.For Jain Americans, this election should be an inspiration rather than merely an occasion for celebration. It should inspire more and more young people from the community to understand government, consider public service, participate in community organizations and develop leadership skills.Representation begins long before someone runs for Congress. School boards, city councils, state legislatures and public commissions offer opportunities to make meaningful contributions.Shah and Dandiya took different paths to Congress, but both demonstrate how professional experience and a commitment to public service can prepare individuals for political leadership.We should encourage political participation across party lines, recognizing that Jain Americans, like other Americans, hold diverse political views. Our shared religious and cultural heritage need not translate into uniform political preferences.The greater goal should be a society in which every individual, regardless of background, has an opportunity to contribute.The November 3 elections offered a powerful reminder that the size of a community need not determine the reach of its influence.For Jain Americans, these victories symbolize the opportunities available to even the smallest communities in a democracy that continues to welcome new voices and perspectives.We may be small in numbers, but the values we bring to American life — and our willingness to serve—can have an impact far beyond our numbers.(Dr Jasvant N Modi is a physician, entrepreneur and philanthropist based in the Los Angeles area. Through the Vardhamana Charitable Foundation, he supports philanthropic initiatives in the United States, India and Europe.)Content courtesy: The American BazaarYou use AI every day. articles.title: US military aircraft leave second UK base
articles.summary: The departures come weeks after the US withdrew bombers from RAF Fairford airbase over a suspected Iran-linked security incident.
articles.body:
At least 10 US Air Force refuelling aircraft left a second airbase in Britain on Monday.

Flight tracking data seen by BBC Verify shows the aircraft left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and landed at other American bases in Europe and also at Prestwick Airport in Ayrshire.

The Wall Street Journal reported that this was in response to a threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified that claim.

Monday's departures come weeks after the US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford airbase over a suspected Iran-linked security incident.

Asked about Monday's flights, an MoD spokesperson told the BBC: "We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly ​according to operational ​requirements."

Using public tracking site Flightradar24 BBC Verify has been able to see USAF KC-135 tankers leaving Mildenhall throughout Monday.

Two aircraft that left initially flew to US bases in Germany and Italy. The first KC-135 then returned to Mildenhall before heading east and landing at Spangdahlem airbase in Germany. The other aircraft - having flown circuits over Aviano airbase in Italy - flew on to and landed at Spangdahlem.

Flight-tracking data also shows eight other US KC-135s left Mildenhall later on Monday.

An aircraft that landed at Prestwick in Scotland on Monday is with the Nebraska Air National Guard, meaning it may have been on a regular stop before heading back to its American base.

Downing Street has insisted that UK airbases are safe following this decision by the US to move some military aircraft to locations in Europe.

The prime minister's official spokesperson said "the protection of our bases, both in the UK and across the world, is a top priority, we work closely with the police and our allies to protect our sites".

About 3,000 military personnel are stationed at RAF Mildenhall, which is around 80 miles (130km) north of London.

The BBC has found there is currently very little aircraft movement at the base, and there appears to be no additional security in place around it. The spaces from which the public can photograph aircraft remain open.

The base is mostly used for refuelling and maintenance operations - flights carrying US presidents, including Donald Trump, have often used it.

It has also been used as a staging area for aircraft and material bound for the Middle East.

Air refuelling tankers were "forward deployed" to the region during operations against Iran.

Asked about the US evacuating aircraft from RAF Mildenhall, Education Secretary Lucy Powell told BBC Breakfast she could not comment on ongoing operational matters.

She added that "we take the security and safety of our bases incredibly seriously" and "we will always act on security intelligence when we need to".

A US Air Force spokesperson said its aircraft "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements".

"US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets," the spokesperson added.

Former UK National Security Adviser Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We are talking about an airbase which houses these large tanker aircraft. Of course, they are large targets, an airbase has a long perimeter, so they are inevitably vulnerable."

He added: "Nobody knows at this stage what this information was. I suspect part of it is an abundance of caution."

Speaking before reports emerged of the flights leaving RAF Mildenhall, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked on Monday about Iranian threats against American diplomats overseas.

"We've addressed it by moving people away from the threat," he said, adding: "Obviously, we're always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas. And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we're going to address it."

Monday's departures from Mildenhall follow a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US-operated airbase in Gloucestershire.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near that base in September. It later emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

Two British nationals appeared in court in October in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot. Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

articles.title: What we know about Alice Huang, the alleged spy at the center of the Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Who is Alice Huang, the woman allegedly at the center of the scandal enveloping the world’s most powerful chip company?
articles.body: Who is Alice Huang, the woman allegedly at the center of the scandal enveloping the world’s most powerful chip company? She’s been photographed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (no relation) at banquet dinners and golf resorts, clinking wine glasses and even leaving an event with him in the same car. But for someone suddenly generating international headlines, she remains something of a mystery. Her limited online footprint paints a picture of a journalist-turned tech power broker who held senior positions at financial firms in Asia. However, US officials believe she was also working as a Chinese spy who was having an affair with the Nvidia chief – and tasked with collecting intelligence on one of the world’s most valuable tech giants in an effort to help Beijing surpass the US in AI dominance. The espionage allegations, combined with an admission of an extramarital affair by the Nvidia chief, have rocked the semiconductor behemoth and the broader chip industry. Here’s what we know about the elusive executive in the middle of it all. What’s her background? US Customs and Border Patrol travel records obtained by CNN that correspond with Alice Huang’s social media posts in the US identify her as a 43-year-old Chinese citizen by the name of Huang Le. According to Chinese social media and databases tracking the career of Huang Le, she worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before pivoting to a career in finance. A report from New York Times described Alice Huang as a fluent English speaker who frequented industry conferences and executive dinners, with connections at the highest levels of the AI industry. One Chinese private-equity fund website said Huang had four years of experience in the media and eight in the securities industry, including at HSBC and Citic Securities. CNN has reached out to HSBC and Citic Securities for comment. From March to November of 2023, Huang was a director at Megaspeed International, according to corporate records in Singapore, where the company is based. The cloud computing and data center provider was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Huang became director and the company changed its name, Megaspeed has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia, purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors by some analyst estimates. Corporate records also indicate Megaspeed received funding from Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and the company has come under investigation for potentially providing Chinese companies with unauthorized access to US chips. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unclear - and she has made no public statement or appearance since last year, when reports of the suspicions surrounding her relationship with Jensen Huang first broke. CNN has reached out to Megaspeed, Singapore’s government and Singaporean police. How does she know Jensen Huang? It is unclear exactly where and when they met, but the Chinese executive has become something of a regular fixture in Huang’s business circles, appearing at the side of the Nvidia CEO at private and corporate events. The two were pictured together as early as September 2024 on WeChat, the ubiquitous Chinese social messaging app, at a luxury golf resort in California. Records from US Customs and Border Protection show Alice Huang has visited the US ten times since 2017. The most recent trip was in March of last year, when she was photographed visiting Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara during the company’s annual conference. In May 2025, the two attended a group dinner in Taipei during a tech conference and left in the same car. Nvidia has previously denied there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about their relationship. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said in statement from October. But on Sunday, the company said it was opening an independent investigation into whether the CEO was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The same weekend Huang admitted to his extramarital affair in a company-wide statement without naming the other party involved. Were any secrets stolen? Nvidia, which is worth about $4.5 trillion and designs some of the world’s most advanced AI chips, said as of Sunday that it has no reason to believe that state or corporate secrets had been compromised. The FBI first raised concerns to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China nearly a year ago, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. The New York Times also reported that intelligence officials were conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang for at least a year, and had briefed President Donald Trump on the matter last year. Trump said he did not regret not taking action, and downplayed Jensen Huang’s culpability in the incident on Monday. He said he believed that the Nvidia CEO was unaware of any potential motivations of espionage. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”

articles.title: What powers does Netanyahu have as Israel’s interim PM?
articles.summary: As Israel faces political gridlock, Netanyahu wields caretaker powers to manage security and disrupt his rivals.
articles.body:
Two weeks after Israel’s national elections, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given a chance by President Isaac Herzog to cobble together a government.

But with neither Eisenkot nor Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition securing the 61 seats needed to secure a majority in the Knesset, who eventually forms the next administration is far from clear.

As Eisenkot huddles with members of his alliance and negotiates with potential outside partners who could support his coalition, including Arab parties, Netanyahu remains ensconced as a caretaker prime minister. And if Eisenkot fails to form a government, Herzog might approach Netanyahu to see if he can form a workable coalition government.

This transitional status creates a unique political landscape where the incumbent lacks a popular mandate but retains the keys to the state’s most powerful institutions.

“Netanyahu lost the priority of forming the government, but he did not lose the current premiership,” Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera. “His power now lies in that his opponents need an agreement to remove him – and their differences are the reason for his current [political] survival.”

In the meantime, Jabareen explained, Israel sits in a “constitutional paradox”: The prime minister does not enjoy a popular mandate.

So what does that mean for Israel, and what powers does Netanyahu enjoy as a caretaker prime minister?

Israel has no single constitution but instead relies on a series of what are known as Basic Laws as its foundational legal principles.

Under Article 30 of Israel’s Basic Law: The Government, the outgoing administration continues to operate seamlessly until there is a new one sworn in to replace it.

“Consequently, Netanyahu and his government continue to work until a new government gains the confidence of the Knesset under the principle of government continuity,” Jabareen said.

“And in this period, the government retains the powers of managing the state, security and foreign relations, but its use is subject to the duty of reservation and restraint.”

The most pressing concern surrounding Netanyahu’s caretaker status is his authority over the military.

He has the authority to make new appointments and security-related decisions. But he is expected to face extra scrutiny over any moves because while he has legal powers, he does not necessarily enjoy “legitimacy” any more, Jabareen noted.

While Netanyahu commands the executive branch, Article 40 of the Basic Law: The Government authorises his cabinet to launch a new war if it votes in its favour. He cannot start a new conflict on his own.

But Netanyahu can strategically manipulate existing conflicts. “The most applicable scenario is not inventing a war from scratch, of course. We are talking about igniting and employing an existing threat. We are talking about Iran. We are talking about Lebanon,” Jabareen said.

Because Eisenkot and his allies are not members of the current security cabinet, Netanyahu wields unchecked influence over how intelligence is framed.

“What is presented to the ministers as a danger that can be contained? And what is presented as a final opportunity [for potential attacks] that cannot be delayed? This additional responsibility of the prime minister regarding the information that reaches the cabinet makes the presentation of options extremely important,” Jabareen explained.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s internal intelligence agency, reports directly to the premier. That does not change while Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister.

While Netanyahu commands security forces, his domestic and legislative powers face functional limits.

Maysara Bahr, a writer and expert on Israeli affairs, explained that financial decisions Netanyahu makes could impact whoever forms the next government.

“Netanyahu can take some actions that may hinder the work of the next government,” so that it inherits greater “indebtedness”, Bahr told Al Jazeera.

However, Netanyahu cannot push through new legislation to protect himself from his long, ongoing corruption trial.

Netanyahu is using his continuing premiership to try to fracture the opposition bloc, Jabareen said.

For instance, the analyst pointed out, Netanyahu is trying to appeal to Zionist voters and parties that represent them by portraying Eisenkot’s alliance as likely to be dependent on Arab parties.

Bahr warned that Netanyahu might encourage domestic unrest to derail the transition, suggesting that the prime minister would do whatever it takes to try to stay in power.

How Israel’s transition compares to other countries

Israel’s transition process is not very different from that in other parliamentary democracies.

In the United Kingdom and India too, for instance, caretaker prime ministers enjoy the same legal powers as premiers with electoral mandates.

However, constitutional conventions and norms require them to avoid major policy decisions – including on questions of war – as caretakers.

In the United States, meanwhile, an outgoing president works under a rigid two-and-a-half-month deadline towards the inauguration of his successor, facing intense congressional oversight regarding transitions, budgets and appointments in the interim.

articles.summary: The United States has evacuated American military aircraft from a military base in England on Monday following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited sources familiar with the matter.
articles.body: The United States has evacuated American military aircraft from a military base in England on Monday following a threat from Iran, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited sources familiar with the matter. The exact threat to the base, Royal Air Force base Mildenhall, remains under discussion by US officials, The WSJ reported. Flight tracking data analyzed by CNN shows that 10 US refueling aircraft were relocated away from RAF Mildenhall on Monday. Four of those KC-135 Stratotankers went to Germany’s Spangdahlem Air Base, one to Germany’s Ramstein Air Base, four to Spain’s Morón Air Base and one to Scotland’s Glasgow Prestwick airport. CNN has reached out to the Pentagon for comment. The United States also upgraded the security threat level at RAF Mildenhall and another airbase RAF Lakenheath to “FPCON Charlie,” according to The WSJ and the defense industry publication The War Zone, citing a US official on Monday. That threat level – the second-highest level in the Pentagon’s force protection system – indicates that some form of terrorist action or targeting action is likely. A UK Ministry of Defense spokesperson said that they “do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.” The spokesperson added that “aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.” The movement of the planes comes after another Iran-linked threat last month to another military base in England, RAF Fairford. RAF Fairford had been used by US B-1 bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five men were arrested outside the base in the early hours of September 27. British prosecutors charged two British nationals under the National Security Act in relation to the incident outside RAF Fairford airbase, with police saying the two were suspected of assisting Iran. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Three workers die at Tata’s iPhone parts plant in India’s Tamil Nadu
articles.summary: The workers had inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank, a district official says.
articles.body:
Three contract workers have died at a Tata Electronics plant producing components for Apple iPhones in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu, the latest incident involving the US tech giant’s supply chain in its most important manufacturing hub outside China.

The deaths occurred at a site in Hosur, in the Krishnagiri district, late on Monday.

The workers were among a group assigned to clean an effluent treatment plant (ETP) at a facility in Hosur, senior district official Dinesh Kumar told The New Indian Express.

Kumar said the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

The three workers were taken to a private hospital, where doctors declared them dead on arrival, TNIE cited Kumar as saying.

The salt-to-aviation Tata Group’s electronics unit accounts for roughly 40 percent of iPhone assembly in India, and Foxconn makes up ‌‌the rest. Tata has in recent months faced many challenges as its iPhone-making operations have been hit by a ransomware attack and concerns about water pollution.

Over the years, as Apple expanded manufacturing beyond China, India has emerged as a key hub, which now accounts for roughly 25 percent of the world’s iPhones.

Tamil Nadu is a key industrial hub in India, hosting factories ⁠⁠of many global giants, such as Foxconn, Hyundai, VinFast and BMW.

The state’s minister for industries, Virudhai Magal Keerthana, said in a post on X that the worker deaths will ⁠⁠be “thoroughly investigated and appropriate action will be taken based on the findings”.

Tata’s Hosur site has faced repeated setbacks: a fire halted production ‌‌at the components plant in 2024, and state authorities warned of a shutdown over alleged groundwater contamination this year before dropping the matter.

Separately, a ransomware breach at an adjacent iPhone plant in the same ‌‌compound ‌‌leaked documents linked to Apple’s then-unreleased iPhone 18 Pro, the Reuters news agency reported previously.

articles.title: In 2023, Washington fined a cattle-ranching couple $267,540 over wetlands they say were stockwater ponds; three years later, they are still fighting restoration demands they estimate could exceed $3.7 million
articles.summary: A Washington cattle-ranching couple has spent three years fighting a $267,540 state penalty and restoration orders they say could cost more than $3.7
articles.body: A Washington cattle-ranching couple has spent three years fighting a $267,540 state penalty and restoration orders they say could cost more than $3.7 million. Wade and Teresa King, who operate King Ranch in Grant and Douglas counties, argue that the sites are longstanding stockwater ponds for their livestock, while the Washington State Department of Ecology says they damaged naturally occurring wetlands, including rare alkali wetlands.The dispute began in February 2023, when Ecology fined the Kings and ordered restoration work near Park Lake in Grant County. In January 2025, the agency issued a second order involving 11 additional wetlands in neighboring Douglas County, bringing the total number of affected sites to 34.What Ecology says happenedEcology’s investigation found that the Kings excavated, recontoured and placed fill in 6.37 acres of naturally occurring wetlands in Grant County. The department says it relied on site visits, soil and water analysis, satellite imagery and aerial photographs dating back to 1949.According to Ecology, the aerial and satellite images showed the wetlands undisturbed until 2021, when the excavation occurred. The agency says many of the sites are rare alkali wetlands, which form in arid eastern Washington when mineral-rich groundwater rises to the surface and mixes with runoff and snowmelt.Ecology says those wetlands can take centuries to form and often dry out during hot weather, leaving bright white salt crusts or playas. The department argues that those seasonal changes do not make the areas artificial ponds, and that the Kings’ actions damaged wetlands protected under Washington’s Water Pollution Control Act of 1945.The agency also says it found no evidence that the water bodies had ever been modified as stockwater ponds. It maintains that formal enforcement involving ranching is rare and that it has no record of previously penalizing a livestock operator solely for damaging wetlands.The Kings’ responseThe Kings reject Ecology’s characterization of the sites. They say the ponds are longstanding stockwater ponds used to provide water for cattle, and that the agency is treating ordinary ranching infrastructure as protected wetlands.Teresa King has said the restoration orders would be financially devastating and practically impossible because the areas were never wetlands in the first place. She and Wade argue that they are being asked to turn non-wetlands into wetlands, a demand they see as both unachievable and unfair.The Kings also say Ecology has not provided enough detail about how they are supposed to comply with the restoration requirements. Wade King argues that the wetlands designation gives the department more authority over the land than it would have if the areas were recognized as stockwater ponds.For the family, the stakes extend beyond money. The Kings have ranched in Grant and Douglas counties since the 1950s, and Teresa says multiple generations now live and work on the property. She describes the fight as a defense of the livestock water rights relied on by ranchers across Washington.The fight over a jury trialThe Kings initially challenged the penalty and restoration orders through Washington’s Pollution Control Hearings Board, an administrative panel that does not offer jury trials. They later filed a separate lawsuit in Grant County Superior Court, arguing that they were entitled to a jury trial and that the administrative process violated that right.In March 2026, a judge dismissed that lawsuit, ruling that the Kings first had to complete the administrative process. The Kings appealed, and in September 2026 the Washington Court of Appeals granted a temporary stay of the Pollution Control Hearings Board proceedings while the appeal continues.Wade King has criticized the administrative process, saying it places too much power in the executive branch and rarely favors property owners. Ecology, meanwhile, says the Kings appealed both the 2023 penalty and the 2025 administrative order, and that the board later required them to grant access to sites they had previously denied inspectors.Oliver Dunford, a senior attorney with the Pacific Legal Foundation representing the Kings, has said they are prepared to take the case to the U.S. Supreme Court if necessary. He argues that the Seventh Amendment should apply against the states and that the Kings should have had a jury trial.The cost of restorationThe Kings’ attorneys estimate that complying with Ecology’s orders could cost more than $3.7 million. That figure is far higher than the original $267,540 penalty and illustrates why the dispute has become so consequential for the family.Ecology says it issued the penalty after repeated attempts to resolve the concerns without formal enforcement. It says the Kings refused to cooperate with those efforts, while the Kings maintain that they have always cared for the land and water their livelihood depends on.The agency says wetlands provide flood and erosion control, recharge groundwater, improve water quality and support plant and animal habitat. It also notes that livestock operators who want to build stock ponds or divert surface water may need local and state permits, water rights or other authorization.Why the case mattersThe King Ranch case has become more than a local land-use dispute. It raises questions about how states balance environmental protection with agricultural operations, and whether property owners facing large penalties should have access to a jury trial.For the Kings, the outcome could determine whether they can continue operating a multigenerational ranch without a restoration bill they believe is impossible to pay. For Ecology, the case is about enforcing protections for wetlands it says were damaged through unauthorized excavation.The case remains unresolved. The Court of Appeals has paused the administrative proceedings while it considers the jury-trial issue, and both sides continue to present sharply different accounts of what the land was before the excavation began.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is Hasina’s game plan as she seeks a passport to return to Bangladesh?
articles.summary: The ousted leader faces the prospect of being hanged upon return for her violent suppression of the 2024 uprising.
articles.body:
Dhaka, Bangladesh – Bangladesh’s ousted leader Sheikh Hasina wants a new passport to return to the country next month, more than two years after fleeing to India following a mass uprising that forced her from power.

The 79-year-old former prime minister was sentenced to death in absentia last year for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on the student-led protests in 2024, a charge she denies.

She faces the prospect of being hanged upon her return, as the government that succeeded her remains a staunch political opponent.

Dhaka has already rejected the passport request and has challenged Hasina to seek extradition from India if she is serious about returning home .

“Bangladesh does not give passports to terrorists who kill thousands of people and flee. It will work under the current extradition arrangements with India to pursue and get the terrorist Hasina handed over,” State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir told Al Jazeera.

On Tuesday, the Bangladeshi prosecutor Md Aminul Islam, who secured the death sentence for Hasina at the Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal, said she will be executed if she returns home.

“Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” Islam told reporters.

So, what led Hasina to approach the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, seeking a new passport and a national identity card since her existing documents have been revoked, and what is her game plan?

Hasina ruled Bangladesh with an iron fist for nearly 20 years and still enjoys support among a section of its population, while many others want to see her hanged.

Her return could worsen political tensions as Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government tries to restore ‌‌stability two years on from the 2024 uprising that led to the killing of more than 1,400 people, according to the United Nations.

But analysts question whether Hasina genuinely intends to return to face the law, or is using the promise to revive her political fortunes from self-imposed exile in India.

For Zillur Rahman, president of the Centre for Governance Studies, a Dhaka-based think tank, Hasina’s passport request is less about an imminent plan to return and more about keeping herself politically relevant as she tries to retain control of her Awami League party.

“I think she knows what her fate is. But what she wants is to keep Awami League leaders and activists politically engaged,” he said, referring to Hasina’s party, which was founded by her father and Bangladesh independence movement leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.

“As far as I understand, she does not want to hand over the party’s leadership to anyone else under any circumstances. I think that is a major problem for her and for the party. Otherwise, the party might have tried to find a way to survive.”

Jon F Danilowicz, a retired United States diplomat who once served as deputy chief of mission at the US embassy in Dhaka, was more categorical.

“There is zero chance that Hasina will return to Bangladesh in December. In my view, this has all been a bluff intended to rally her supporters and shift the narrative regarding her increasing irrelevance at home,” he told Al Jazeera.

Faiz Sobhan, senior research director at the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute research centre, also sees Hasina’s promise as an effort to lift the morale of her party, which is now banned, with many of its leaders in jail or in exile.

“The announcement keeps Sheikh Hasina politically relevant and lets her gauge the mood at home,” he said. “An actual return seems inconceivable, since it would mean facing the gallows or spending the rest of her life behind bars.”

Despite analysts casting doubt on the prospect of Hasina’s return, her announcement appears to have energised some Awami League leaders and supporters.

“Our leader will return. They have tried to stop her before, but they could not stop her. They are conspiring against her again, but she will overcome these conspiracies and return,” an organising secretary of the party’s central executive committee told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity from exile in India.

When asked how Hasina would return and what steps the party was taking to facilitate it, many Awami League leaders and supporters said they had no clear idea about her game plan.

“But she has announced that she will return, and I believe she will come back in December, no matter what,” Arman Rahman, a Dhaka-based Awami League activist and former leader of its student wing, told Al Jazeera.

Hasina’s future is also tied to India’s calculations.

New Delhi, her close ally for decades, has sheltered her since she fled Dhaka in August 2024. But her continued presence has become a point of contention between the two countries.

Dhaka has repeatedly sought Hasina’s extradition under a bilateral treaty. New Delhi says it has been examining the requests, with India’s foreign ministry in April saying it wants to “engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties”.

Meanwhile, both countries have signalled an interest in repairing strained ties.

Sreeradha Datta, professor of international affairs at O P Jindal Global University near New Delhi, told Al Jazeera that India regards Hasina as a longstanding friend, even as it tries to separate her presence in the country from its diplomatic engagement with Dhaka.

“Sheikh Hasina is a very good friend of India. [New] Delhi looks at her as a friend whom it will always support. That is our official position,” she said.

Former US diplomat Danilowicz believes New Delhi is increasingly aware of the diplomatic cost of continuing to host Hasina, but is “unlikely to facilitate” her return to Bangladesh.

“While there may be some in India who still believe that Hasina and her party provide them leverage, by now the [Narendra] Modi government must understand the damage that her continued presence in New Delhi is doing to efforts to normalise relations with Bangladesh,” he said.

“I am certain the Modi government would love to see the Hasina problem go away, including by having her find a third country to reside.”

Rahman, of the Centre for Governance Studies, offered a different explanation for why India may continue to shelter Hasina despite the diplomatic complications.

“I think India is finding it difficult to digest her presence, but at the same time, it cannot let her go either,” he said.

“If India does not take responsibility for protecting her now, its other allies in South Asia and elsewhere may lose trust in New Delhi. They may feel that India does not ultimately protect those who have stood by it.”

Rahman believes India may continue to offer Hasina refuge, but is unlikely to help restore her political domain in Bangladesh.

“I don’t think India will abandon her. But at the same time, I don’t think it will provide her with all forms of political protection, particularly by helping her return to Bangladesh and reestablish herself here,” he said.

Datta, meanwhile, does not expect imminent improvement in relations between the neighbours. “I don’t think Bangladesh-India relations will return to normalisation very soon,” he said.

Many are also asking if Hasina could enter into some kind of a political understanding with the governing Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), now controlled by Prime Minister Rahman, son of Hasina’s longtime rival, Khaleda Zia, who passed away a year ago. Rahman himself lived in exile in London when Hasina was in power.

But analysts see little possibility of such a deal, with the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute’s Sobhan describing the idea as a “non-starter”.

“The BNP has little to gain and much to lose from any accommodation with the Awami League. Its base spent 16-plus years being jailed, harassed and sidelined [by Hasina], and any hint of a deal would be seen as a betrayal,” he told Al Jazeera.

On Monday, BNP acting secretary general and Prime Minister Rahman’s political adviser, Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, also dismissed the prospect of Hasina’s return.

“She is deluding herself if she thinks she can return, reimpose fascism and reclaim her throne,” Rizvi said at an event in Dhaka.

Sobhan said the BNP government had little room to act outside the verdict delivered by the International Crimes Tribunal.

“A broader settlement to stabilise the country is hard to imagine, and reconciliation without accountability or an apology is harder still,” he said.

Extradition was the “only formal route” available to Dhaka, Sobhan added. “And it means being dragged back [to Bangladesh], not choosing to return.”

articles.title: U.S.-mediated talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine begin in Abu Dhabi
articles.summary: Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow’s all-out invasion nearly five years ago.
articles.body: Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington renews its push to end the war that followed Moscow’s all-out invasion nearly five years ago. The two-day session in the UAE’s capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on security guarantees, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions. Hopes of progress in ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say. There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks took place against a backdrop of new long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line. Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said. Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a “negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment.” The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, noted at the start of the talks that the Russian delegation “has become bigger and more professional.” He expressed hope that the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.” Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who is leading Kyiv’s delegation, said that the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission. The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine. Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was visiting Denmark on Tuesday, rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia hasn’t been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine’s military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again. Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks. Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff’s operational department, Yuri Zhigarlovsky. Apart from Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party. Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.” Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.” The discussions in Abu Dhabi will set the stage for “that engagement to begin in the near future, as part of a broader multilateral process,” he said. Moscow has praised the broad approach. “We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump’s request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said. Just before Moscow launched the full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the trans-Atlantic alliance’s member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia. Kushner said that before the start of the three-way talks, he and Witkoff would meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to “continue the close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.” Some in the EU see Washington’s proposals as too accommodating to Moscow. Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said that EU representatives could join at a later stage. While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles. Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to weaken the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors. Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: Keira Knightley’s unforgettable green ‘Atonement’ dress is going up for sale
articles.summary: Almost two decades after Keira Knightley bewitched audiences in the 2007 film, “Atonement,” the emerald-green silk dress she wore in a pivotal scene is coming up for auction.
articles.body: Almost two decades after Keira Knightley bewitched audiences in the 2007 film, “Atonement,” the emerald-green silk dress she wore in a pivotal scene is coming up for auction. Thanks to its enduring allure, the backless gown designed by Jacqueline Durran is expected to sell for up to £120,000 ($161,000) when it goes under the hammer at Christie’s in London on December 9. Knightley’s character, Cecilia, wore the dress in a climactic scene in Joe Wright’s adaptation of Ian McEwan’s tragic romance novel. During the scene, Cecilia makes love with the housekeeper’s son Robbie (played by James McAvoy) in the grand home library after weeks of romantic tension, and they confess their feelings for one another. “When we started making the movie, we all knew it was a pivotal moment, and it had to be a memorable dress,” Durran told Entertainment Weekly in an interview published in 2017. “Joe (Wright) said that to me, right at the beginning, which was obviously a lot of pressure on me to try and make this memorable dress,” she continued. “But we didn’t know, really. It was a complete surprise how much it did resonate with people and how much it was picked out as a single look from the movie.” “When the film came out in 2007, I just remember so much about that dress,” Caroline Young, author of the 2022 book “The Color of Fashion: The Story of Clothes in Ten Colors,” told CNN. “It’s glamorous, it’s nostalgic, and that green is so significant,” she added. “Green has a deep history of representing tempestuous love and illicit affairs,” Young wrote in her book, adding that the “Atonement” gown is “one of the most talked about green dresses in recent years.” “Because that segment of the film was set in the 1930s,” Young told CNN, the dress “has this Jean Harlow-esque quality — the sort of slinkiness of the cut, the thin straps.” “It’s this perfect summer before tragedy strikes,” Young added. ‘Instantly recognizable’ Wright had various instructions for Durran for the dress design, including that “it should have movement at the hem and be quite full-skirted,” Durran said. He “wanted it as showstopping as we could make it, and that it should be green,” although he “wasn’t specific” about the shade, and “the mood of the dress should be that it could remind the audience that it is the hottest day of the year.” For this reason, Durran said she tried to make the dress from “very fine fabric, and make it very light and unstructured.” She drew on reference books from the 1920s and ‘30s and “pulled out things that I thought would suit Keira.” The emerald gown, “brought to life with exquisite artistry on screen” now stands as “one of the most instantly recognizable” dresses in fashion history, Thais Hitchins, head of sale at Christie’s London, said in a statement shared with CNN, adding that the gown is an “emblem of desire, lust and heartbreaking romance.” Following the movie, the dress was taken from the production archive and sold at a charity auction in 2008, and it has remained in an American private collection since, a spokesperson for Christie’s told CNN. “Coming up to 20 years since the film’s release, it’s a poignant time to revisit the iconic dress and shine a spotlight on this incredible piece of fashion history,” they added. While it is “difficult to predict” who will bid for the dress, the spokesperson said they expect the dress to appeal to individual collectors with a particular interest in “Atonement” and those passionate about film and costume history, as well as museums and institutions, given the gown’s cultural significance. The garment will be sold as part of the “Love & Lust: A Literary Guide” sale. Other items in the sale include the artworks for the release posters of the 1927 sci-fi film “Metropolis” and 1931 vampire horror “Dracula,” three autograph letters written by British naval hero Horatio Nelson to his mistress Emma, Lady Hamilton, and the original costume worn by English prima ballerina Margot Fonteyn as Princess Aurora in a 1960 production of “The Sleeping Beauty.” Film fashion is highly sought after at international auction houses. Audrey Hepburn’s black Italian satin dress, designed by Hubert de Givenchy for the 1961 romantic comedy “Breakfast at Tiffany’s,” sold at Christie’s in 2006 for £467,200 (equivalent to around $920,000 at the time), more than six times its estimated value. Hepburn’s personal collection of her clothes and memorabilia then went up for auction at Christie’s in London in 2017, selling for a total of £4,635,500 ($6.2 million). In 2015, a dress worn by Vivien Leigh in “Gone With the Wind” also fetched $137,000.

articles.title: U.S. moves military aircraft from British base amid Iran threats
articles.summary: The United States has moved military aircraft from the RAF Mildenhall airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran.
articles.body: LONDON — The United States has moved military aircraft from an airbase in the United Kingdom amid threats from Iran. A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased. They were operating under “enhanced force protection measures,” the official said. They would not speculate on the exact nature of the threat that appears to have led to ramped up security. At least eight air refueling tankers and three Ospreys left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed. Some of the tankers, Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers, were relocated to airbases in Germany and Spain, with one moved to the area of Glasgow Prestwick Airport in Scotland. The Ospreys were moved to nearby RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk. It comes weeks after the U.S. withdrew bombers from another base in Britain, RAF Fairford, after police foiled a suspected terror plot linked to Iran. The U.S. has used bases in the U.K. to strike the Islamic Republic. The Wall Street Journal was first to report on this week’s movements and said the evacuation came following a threat from Iran, citing people familiar with the matter. It said the exact nature of the threat was not yet known and remained under discussion by U.S. officials. “We take proactive measures to ensure our aircraft, our people, and our installations remain safe and secure,” a U.S. official told NBC News. “U.S. Air Force aircraft rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirement,” a U.S. European Command official said. “U.S. military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our Allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets,” the European Command official added. A spokesperson for the U.K.’s Ministry of Defense said it does “not routinely comment on the activity of other nations.” “Aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements,” the spokesperson said. It comes weeks after the U.S. pulled aircraft from RAF Fairford following reports of a possible Iranian drone attack, two U.S. officials previously told NBC News. That move came in the wake of an investigation into a possible planned terrorist attack at that base, located in Gloucestershire. Five men were detained on Sept. 27 after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward RAF Fairford. Other arrests followed and two men were charged under the National Security Act. The incident, which attracted huge international attention, remains largely unexplained although British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the activity was likely to have been coordinated in Iran. Though Tehran has denied involvement in any plot against RAF Fairford, its powerful Revolutionary Guard warned in July that any base used to launch attacks against Iranian territory was a legitimate target. Iran has vowed retaliation for any renewal of the American-Israeli war against it and has threatened to expand its response beyond the Middle East. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington had addressed concerns around reported threats from Tehran against American diplomats overseas by “moving people away from the threat.” “Obviously, we’re always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas,” Rubio said. “And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we’re going to address it.” Citing new “momentum” in negotiations to end the war, President Donald Trump on Monday downplayed the prospect of new U.S. attacks. “Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said following a meeting with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani. Further U.S. attacks “won’t be necessary” at this point, but Washington remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change, Trump told reporters at the White House.

articles.title: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge ‘sabotage’
articles.summary: The French government said it is seeking tough sanctions to deter further cyberattacks across Europe.
articles.body:
France says it has summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris “to lodge a very strong protest” after it accused Tehran of carrying out a major cyberattack targeting supermarket fridges last month.

“It marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation’s interests and the security of the French people,” Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday.

“I can also tell you that we rule nothing out and will take all measures – including those we may not disclose publicly – that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks,” he added.

Barrot, speaking on France Info ‌‌television, said the government would push for European Union sanctions in response to what he called an “attack of unprecedented scale and aggression in our country”.

He said firm measures would be taken “to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again”.

On Monday, Barrot said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind cyberattacks targeting more than 700 French supermarkets on October 11 and 12, when refrigerators were remotely accessed “to initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles”.

Raised temperatures in fridges forced the supermarkets to throw away all perishable food.

Millions of euros’ worth of food was spoiled, according to retailers. In some cases, the raised temperatures sparked fires or melted equipment.

French supermarket groups E-Leclerc, Intermarche, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U were all hit.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday she had opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit of the IRGC, over the attacks.

The prosecutor’s office has requested international arrest warrants be issued for two Shahid Kaveh officials.

Similar incidents have since been reported in other European countries.

In a suspected cyberattack on November 2, temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden.

Jody Westby, chief executive of Global Cyber Risk LLC, said tracking down the group directly responsible for the attacks is “very difficult” because of poor cooperation on international cybercrime investigations.

“It’s been a problem for 20 some years, and now it’s a little better, but only marginally so,” Westby told Al Jazeera. She said that it was difficult to track and trace the origin of such attacks “because of the nature of packet switching”.

In recent days, European air traffic has also been disrupted by false bomb alerts against dozens of flights, although the origin of those threats has yet to be determined.
